title: How an IoC container wires objects
idea: An IoC container is a library that builds your object graph: it reads which classes exist, resolves each constructor's parameters by type, and hands back ready objects.
points: Spring finds beans by component scanning (`@Component`, `@Service`) or `@Bean` methods.
It resolves constructor parameters by type, building dependencies first, recursively.
Beans are singletons by default: one shared instance per container, so keep them stateless.
Wiring errors (missing, ambiguous or cyclic beans) fail at startup for eager singletons.

hero.title: One get() call, resolved depth first

steps.caption: `bind` records that the `PaymentGateway` role is played by `FakeGateway`. Nothing is built yet.
`get(OrderService.class)`: no binding, so the class itself is used. It is not cached, so building starts.
Its constructor needs a `PaymentGateway`. The binding says build `FakeGateway`, so it goes on the stack.
`FakeGateway` takes no parameters. It is created and cached as a singleton.
The second parameter is `AuditLog`, a concrete class. It is built the same way.
`AuditLog` is cached too. Every parameter of `OrderService` now exists.
The container calls the constructor with both objects: constructor injection, done by code you did not write.
A second `get(OrderService.class)` finds the cached singleton and returns the same instance.

code.title: A toy container
code.caption: A toy container with the same core moves as Spring: bindings, recursive resolution, singletons, startup errors.

walk.text: Bindings map a role to a class. Singletons cache built objects. `inProgress` tracks the current path.
`get` resolves the binding, then returns the cached object or builds a new one.
Reflection finds the single constructor, builds each parameter first, then calls it.
Fail fast: an interface with no binding, or a class already on the path, means a cycle.
`main` binds one role and asks for the top object. The container builds the rest.
An empty container hits the missing binding; `Inventory` and `Pricing` need each other.

code.title: The same graph in Spring
code.caption: Annotations replace `bind`; Spring scans, builds and caches the beans at startup.

walk.text: `@Component` marks a class for component scanning. Spring registers it as a singleton bean.
`@Service` is a `@Component` with a clearer name. The fields stay `final`.
With one constructor, Spring injects it without `@Autowired`, matching each parameter by type.
`SpringApplication.run` scans, wires the graph and returns the context. `getBean` only proves it; real code gets injected.

pitfalls: Two beans for one single-valued parameter fail startup as ambiguous; pick one with `@Primary` or `@Qualifier`.
Mutable fields in a singleton bean are shared by every request thread.
Calling `new` on a `@Service` yourself skips the container; its dependencies stay unset.

quiz.q: You add `StripeGateway` as a second `@Component` implementing `PaymentGateway`. What happens at startup?
options: Spring picks the first class it scanned
Startup fails: two beans match PaymentGateway
Both are injected as a list automatically
The last scanned class silently wins
quiz.why: Injection matches by type. Neither bean is `@Primary` and neither name matches the parameter `gateway`, so the candidates are ambiguous and startup fails until `@Qualifier` picks one.

takeaway: A container automates constructor injection: scan, resolve by type, cache singletons.
